prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The bodies of young elephants covered in the brown dirt of dried-up wells tell a heartrending story. A baby elephant in the Gourma region of central Mali had been trapped in a well for three days. Reaching desperately for drops of water, they had lowered their trunks, toppled in, remained trapped and died in Mali's scorching heat. The "last desert elephants in West Africa" have "adapted to survive in the harsh conditions" they face, Save the Elephants said Monday. But now, the group says, conditions have gone from bad to worse, and they are living "on the margin of what is ecologically viable." Save the Elephants distributed new pictures Monday that depict the devastating drought and the struggle for survival in Mali, one of the poorest nations in the world. "Six elephants have already been found dead," the group wrote in a news release accompanying the photos. "Four others, including three calves, were recently extracted from a shallow well into which they had fallen when searching for water. Only the largest survived." The youngest are in the most danger, since their smaller trunks can't reach deep into the few remaining wells, the group said. The worst drought in 26 years is threatening the existence of the "last desert elephants in West Africa," the northernmost herds in the continent, Save the Elephants said. The animals, now numbering only about 350 to 450, have been called "the last elephants of Timbuktu," said Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants. But they're south of Timbuktu, Wall told CNN in a phone interview from Bamako, Mali. "We tend to refer to them as 'the last Sahelian elephants.' "  See a map of Mali » . Each year, the elephants trek farther on the fringes of the Sahara to find water. They have the longest migration route of any in the continent, traveling "in a counterclockwise circle" of about 700 kilometers (435 miles), Save the Elephants said. The images are signs of the crisis gripping the northwest African nation. The U.N. Development Programme ranks Mali near the bottom of its Human Development Index. It cites a 56 percent poverty rate in the country, with nearly a third of the population unlikely to live past age 40, and an illiteracy rate of 77 percent. The World Food Programme says the majority of infant deaths in Mali are due to malnutrition. The drought, combined with soaring temperatures, has also led to deaths of cattle, Save the Elephants said. "The stench of rotting corpses fills the air, and what little water remains is putrid and undrinkable by all standards." In areas where the elephants live and search for water, "the normal peaceful coexistence between the elephants and herdsmen is starting to break down and giving way to conflict over access to water," Wall said. There is some hope for the weeks and months ahead. "We're hoping the rains start in June, and that will allow the elephants to start drinking out of shallow ponds until the really heavy rains begin" in July or August, Wall said. But "urgent action" is needed in the interim "to secure water for the elephants," Wall's group said in its news release. Save the Elephants, which focuses on helping elephant populations worldwide, said it has partnered with a foundation and the Mali government in its fundraising appeal.

(CNN) — The bodies of young elephants, coated with the brown soil of dried-out wells, reveal a tragic struggle for survival. In central Mali’s Gourma region, one calf remained trapped in a well for three days. Desperate for water, elephants stretch their trunks toward the last drops, lose their footing, fall inside and eventually die in the country’s extreme heat.

Save the Elephants said Monday that West Africa’s remaining desert elephants have evolved to endure severe conditions. The organization warned, however, that the situation has deteriorated so dramatically that the animals are now surviving at the edge of ecological viability.

On Monday, the group released new photographs documenting the destructive drought and the elephants’ fight to stay alive in Mali, one of the world’s poorest countries. A statement issued with the images said six elephants had already been discovered dead. Four more—including three calves—were recently pulled from a shallow well after falling in while looking for water, but only the largest animal survived.

Calves face the greatest risk because their short trunks cannot reach far enough into the few wells that still contain water, according to the organization.

Save the Elephants said the most severe drought in 26 years is endangering West Africa’s last desert elephants, which are also the continent’s northernmost herds. Their population is estimated at just 350 to 450.

Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants, said the animals have sometimes been described as the “last elephants of Timbuktu.” In a telephone interview with CNN from Bamako, Mali, he clarified that they actually live south of Timbuktu and are more commonly called the last Sahelian elephants.

Every year, the herds travel increasingly far along the Sahara’s margins in search of water. Save the Elephants said they follow an approximately 700-kilometer—or 435-mile—counterclockwise circuit, the longest elephant migration route in Africa.

The photographs also reflect the wider emergency affecting the northwestern African country. Mali is ranked close to the bottom of the United Nations Development Programme’s Human Development Index. According to the agency, 56% of Malians live in poverty, nearly one-third are not expected to survive beyond age 40, and 77% of the population is illiterate. The World Food Programme reports that malnutrition causes most infant deaths in the country.

Save the Elephants said the combination of drought and rapidly rising temperatures has killed cattle as well. Rotting carcasses have left a powerful odor in the air, while the small amount of water that remains is contaminated and unsuitable for drinking.

Wall said that in places where elephants and pastoralists seek the same limited water supplies, their traditionally peaceful relationship is beginning to deteriorate into competition and conflict.

There is still some reason for optimism in the coming weeks and months. Wall said the group hopes rainfall will begin in June, allowing the elephants to drink from shallow pools until heavier rains arrive in July or August.

Until then, Save the Elephants said immediate measures are necessary to provide the herds with secure access to water. The international elephant-conservation organization added that it is working with a foundation and Mali’s government on an appeal to raise funds.

**Drought pushes West Africa’s last desert elephants closer to the brink**

**BAMAKO, Mali —** A severe drought in Mali is shrinking water holes and stripping vegetation across the country’s Gourma region, threatening what conservationists describe as West Africa’s last population of desert-adapted elephants.

The elephants survive by moving between scattered sources of water and food along an annual migration route of roughly 600 kilometers, according to Save the Elephants. The conservation group calls the herd “the last remaining population of desert-adapted elephants in West Africa.”

Only a few hundred are believed to remain. Save the Elephants has previously put the population at about 250 animals, following years of poaching, armed conflict and habitat loss.

Now, prolonged dry conditions are adding pressure. As ponds disappear and pasture deteriorates, elephants must travel farther to drink, increasing the risk of exhaustion and bringing them into closer contact with villages, livestock and armed groups.

“The Gourma elephants undertake one of the longest elephant migrations in Africa,” Save the Elephants says, describing a circular journey through an arid landscape where access to water determines their survival.

Drought also intensifies competition between wildlife and communities whose cattle, goats and crops depend on the same limited resources. Conservationists warn that encounters can turn deadly when elephants damage fields or enter settlements in search of water.

Mali’s continuing insecurity makes protection more difficult. Rangers and local conservation teams often operate in areas affected by militant violence, trafficking and weak government control. Save the Elephants has documented how poaching sharply reduced the herd during the past decade, leaving the survivors increasingly vulnerable to environmental shocks.

Local initiatives have focused on protecting migration corridors, monitoring wells and involving communities in decisions over land and water. But conservationists say emergency measures — including safeguarding key water points and reducing disturbance around them — may be necessary if the drought continues.

For Mali’s desert elephants, the crisis is about more than a single dry season. With such a small population, the death of even a few animals can have lasting consequences.

Their disappearance would erase not only West Africa’s final desert-adapted elephant herd, but also a unique migration shaped by generations of survival in one of the continent’s harshest landscapes.

counterfactuals.output:
# Mali’s Last Sahelian Elephants Struggle for Water as Drought Tightens Its Grip

In Mali’s vast Gourma region, where the Sahara gives way to the dry grasslands of the Sahel, one of Africa’s most remarkable elephant populations is fighting to survive.

Often described as Mali’s “last Sahelian elephants,” these animals endure conditions far harsher than those faced by elephants in wetter savannas. Each year, they travel hundreds of kilometres through an increasingly unforgiving landscape, following an ancient circuit between seasonal lakes, grazing areas and scattered water points.

But that migration is becoming more dangerous. Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, insecurity and growing pressure from livestock are shrinking the elephants’ options. Wells and ponds that once provided water late into the dry season are failing. In some places, elephants have died after reaching water points only to find them dry or inaccessible. Others have become trapped or injured around deep, unprotected wells as they search desperately for moisture.

The survival of the herd now depends heavily on the arrival of the rainy season.

## A herd adapted to extremes

Mali’s elephants are sometimes called “desert elephants,” although their habitat is more accurately described as Sahelian—a broad belt of semi-arid grassland and scrub stretching across Africa south of the Sahara.

They live mainly in the Gourma, a remote region south of the Niger River and near the border with Burkina Faso. Unlike elephants in protected parks with permanent rivers, the Gourma animals must keep moving to survive. Their annual migration is commonly described as a roughly 600-kilometre circuit, although the distance travelled by individual groups can vary depending on rainfall, vegetation and access to water.

During the dry season, the elephants gather around the few lakes, marshes and wells that still hold water. When rains return, they disperse across a wider area, feeding on newly grown grasses, leaves and woody vegetation.

This movement is not random. Older elephants—especially experienced matriarchs—carry knowledge of routes and water sources passed down over generations. In a normal year, that memory can guide the herd through the leanest months. In an abnormal year, however, even a remembered water point may have disappeared.

## Wells that no longer provide refuge

The drying of wells is one of the most visible signs of the crisis.

Across the Sahel, communities rely on hand-dug wells and boreholes for people and livestock. Elephants also approach these sites, particularly when natural ponds evaporate. Yet a well that appears promising may contain too little water, may be too deep for an elephant to reach safely, or may have collapsed as the surrounding soil dried.

Deaths associated with dried-up wells illustrate the animals’ desperation. Elephants can walk long distances and tolerate difficult conditions, but they require enormous quantities of water. Adults may drink well over 100 litres in a day when water is available, and lactating females and calves are especially vulnerable when shortages persist.

A failed water point can therefore become a death trap in more than one sense. Animals may arrive already weakened by heat and thirst. They may crowd around a narrow opening, break unstable ground or slip into an excavation. Calves face particular danger because they lack the strength and reach of adults.

Such deaths are not isolated natural tragedies. They are evidence that the network of water sources supporting both wildlife and people is breaking down.

## Elephants and herders at the same shrinking water holes

The elephants are not alone in their struggle. Pastoralist communities in northern and central Mali depend on cattle, goats, sheep and camels. When rainfall is poor, herders must drive their animals farther in search of pasture and water—often toward the same remaining lakes and wells used by elephants.

Competition is most intense near the end of the dry season. Thousands of livestock may gather around a single water point, trampling vegetation and consuming water faster than it can be replenished. Elephants arriving at these sites can frighten people and animals, damage wells or water equipment, and consume large volumes in a short period.

For herders, the danger is immediate. A single encounter can scatter livestock, destroy a family’s limited supplies or put lives at risk. For elephants, the presence of people and cattle can block access to a water source they need to survive.

This does not mean that conflict is inevitable. Communities in the Gourma have long lived alongside elephants and possess detailed knowledge of their movements. Local conservation initiatives have sought to establish committees, protect migration corridors, monitor water points and reduce confrontations. In some areas, residents have helped report poaching or avoid key elephant routes during sensitive periods.

But coexistence becomes harder when there is not enough water for everyone.

## Climate pressure compounded by insecurity

Drought is only one part of the threat.

Mali has faced years of armed conflict, political instability and displacement. Insecurity can prevent conservation teams from reaching remote locations, disrupt wildlife monitoring and make it difficult to repair wells or maintain pumps. Weapons circulating through conflict zones also increase the risk of poaching.

At the same time, displaced people and livestock may move into areas already under environmental stress. Farming, charcoal production and the cutting of trees can further reduce the vegetation available to elephants and close off parts of their migration route.

Elephants need more than isolated reserves. They require connected landscapes large enough to accommodate seasonal movement. Roads, settlements, cultivated fields and insecurity can turn their annual circuit into a series of bottlenecks. If even one crucial lake or corridor becomes inaccessible, the effects may be felt across the entire migration.

Climate change intensifies these pressures. The Sahel has always experienced dramatic swings between drought and rain, but increasingly irregular seasons make traditional patterns less reliable. Rain may arrive late, fall in violent bursts that run off hardened soil, or end before ponds and aquifers have been replenished.

A storm can green the landscape briefly without restoring the deeper water reserves needed to carry animals and people through the next dry season.

## The long wait for rain

For the elephants, the rainy season offers the clearest hope of relief.

When sustained rains arrive, temporary pools refill, grasses emerge and the herd can spread out. Competition at permanent water points eases, and females with calves gain access to better forage. Herders, too, can move livestock away from the most crowded wells as pasture becomes available across a wider area.

Yet the first clouds do not end the danger. Rain must fall in the right places and in sufficient amounts. A few showers may cool the air but do little to restore depleted wells. Flooding can also damage infrastructure or cut off routes.

Conservationists therefore view the rains as both a lifeline and a reminder: the herd cannot depend indefinitely on good fortune. Protecting the elephants will require maintaining safe water points, securing migration corridors, reducing the risk posed by open wells and working with pastoralist communities whose own survival depends on the same land.

## A shared struggle for survival

The plight of Mali’s elephants is sometimes framed as a contest between wildlife and people. In reality, elephants and herders are being squeezed by many of the same forces: failing rains, degraded pasture, insecurity and the disappearance of dependable water.

Any lasting solution must account for both.

Strategically located boreholes and better-managed wells could reduce crowding, but new water infrastructure must be planned carefully so it does not encourage permanent settlement or overgrazing in sensitive habitat. Dangerous wells can be reinforced or covered, while escape ramps and other safeguards may help prevent animals from becoming trapped. Early-warning systems can inform communities when elephants are approaching, and local monitoring networks can help keep migration routes open.

Above all, residents must be treated as partners. Protecting elephants without addressing the needs of herders is unlikely to work; supporting livestock without preserving wildlife corridors could push the herd toward extinction.

Mali’s Sahelian elephants have survived centuries of climatic extremes by moving, remembering and adapting. Their annual migration is a testament to resilience. But resilience has limits. As wells dry and competition for water grows, each delayed rainy season brings the herd closer to those limits.

For now, people and elephants alike look to the horizon for darkening clouds—and hope that this year the rains will come in time.

counterfactuals.output:
## Young elephants perish as Mali endures worst drought in 26 years

Newly released photographs from northern Mali show the bodies of young elephants that died as the country’s most severe drought in 26 years depleted watering holes and withered vegetation across the Sahel.

The images highlight the vulnerability of Mali’s desert elephants, a small and internationally important population living mainly in the Gourma region. The herd follows a long seasonal migration between scattered sources of water and forage. Calves are particularly at risk when pools dry early: they cannot travel as far as adults, tolerate heat as well, or compete successfully for limited water.

Conservationists warn that drought is only one of several pressures on the elephants. Livestock and people increasingly depend on the same wells, lakes and grazing areas, while land degradation, settlement and insecurity have disrupted traditional migration routes. When surface water disappears, elephants may crowd around the few remaining sources, increasing the danger of dehydration, disease and conflict with local communities.

### A wider human emergency

The drought is also worsening hardship for Mali’s population. Mali is among the world’s poorest countries, with many families dependent on rain-fed farming, herding and seasonal labor. Rural communities have little protection when rains fail: harvests decline, animals lose weight or die, food prices rise and household income collapses.

Malnutrition—especially among young children—is a persistent problem. During droughts and the annual pre-harvest “lean season,” families often reduce the number or quality of meals. Limited access to clean water, sanitation and health care can intensify acute malnutrition because illnesses such as diarrhea and malaria prevent children from absorbing nutrients.

### Harsh environmental conditions

Much of Mali lies within the Sahara or the semi-arid Sahel. Rainfall is low, highly variable and concentrated in a short wet season. Recurrent drought, soil erosion, overgrazing and the loss of trees have reduced the land’s ability to retain water and support crops or pasture. Climate change is expected to bring greater heat and rainfall volatility, although individual droughts result from a combination of natural climate patterns and long-term warming.

The photographs therefore document more than the deaths of elephant calves. They show how the same environmental shock can threaten wildlife, livestock and people simultaneously. Aid agencies and conservation groups say emergency food, water and veterinary assistance must be paired with longer-term measures such as protecting elephant corridors, managing shared water points, restoring degraded land and helping communities withstand increasingly erratic rainfall.

counterfactuals.output:
**Extreme heat, drought threaten Mali’s last desert elephants near Timbuktu**

**TIMBUKTU, Mali —** Prolonged drought and punishing temperatures are putting one of the world’s last populations of desert-adapted elephants under severe pressure, with an estimated 350 to 450 animals remaining in Mali’s Gourma region, south and east of Timbuktu.

Water holes and grazing areas used by the elephants are shrinking as extreme heat intensifies evaporation and reduces vegetation. The animals must travel increasingly long distances between seasonal water and food sources, raising the risk of dehydration, exhaustion and conflict with communities competing for the same scarce resources.

Jake Wall, a scientist with Save the Elephants who studies elephant movement, said tracking data can help researchers identify critical migration corridors and water sources. He warned that drought becomes especially dangerous when elephants’ traditional routes are blocked or disturbed, leaving them fewer options as conditions deteriorate.

The Gourma elephants are known for making vast seasonal journeys across the Sahel to survive in an exceptionally arid landscape. Scientists and conservation groups say protecting access to water, preserving migration corridors and working with local communities will be essential to keeping the isolated population alive.

The climate threat comes on top of insecurity and human pressure in northern Mali, which have complicated monitoring and conservation work. Young elephants and nursing mothers are considered particularly vulnerable when water and forage disappear.

Conservationists caution that the population estimate is approximate because the elephants range across a large, remote and often inaccessible area. But they say the trend is clear: a herd already numbering only in the hundreds has little margin for additional losses.

*Editor’s note: Any direct quotation from Jake Wall should be checked against an interview, statement or published source before release; the comments above are paraphrased to avoid fabricating remarks.*
